report.source_text:
Finally, a diagnosis of tuberculosis of the first metatarsal of the left foot with bilateral congenital hallux valgus without pulmonary involvement was made, and she was put on anti-tubercular treatment per her weight initially with four drugs (56 doses) and followed with three drugs for a period of 10 months (Table 1). Along with this she was given a tablet of pyridoxine 1 mg/kg/day for the full course duration and was given dietary advice for a high protein diet. An orthopedician was consulted for her hallux valgus who decided to continue with non-operative management until the closure of physis and advised shoe modifications, besides her parents were reluctant to any surgery.
For the first two months, she responded well to the anti-tubercular treatment with no major adverse drug events, and at the request of her parents, she was transferred out to her village.

clinician.final_diagnosis: tuberculosis of the first metatarsal of the left foot with bilateral congenital hallux valgus without pulmonary involvement
clinician.trajectory_summary: An eight-year-old female presented with chronic pain and a purulent discharging wound over the plantar aspect of her left foot for six months, along with a limp and pre-existing bilateral hallux valgus. Physical examination revealed a 4x5 cm wound with an active purulent sinus over the first metatarsal, inflammation, and limited painful movement of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Imaging (X-ray and MRI) showed an expansile osteolytic lesion with cortical thinning, a lytic lesion (16x19 mm) in the first metatarsal head and distal shaft, a bony sequestrum, and a sinus tract. Laboratory tests revealed a raised ESR (55 mm/hr), while other serological indicators were normal. Sputum AFB and CBNAAT were negative, and a chest radiograph was unremarkable, ruling out pulmonary involvement. Histopathological examination of the tissue from the lesion confirmed tuberculosis, showing epitheloid granulomas with caseating necrosis and lymphocytes. Following diagnosis, the patient was initiated on anti-tubercular treatment (four drugs initially, then three drugs for 10 months) and responded well within the first two months. Non-operative management was advised for the hallux valgus.

final.trajectory_summary: An eight-year-old female presented with chronic pain and a purulent discharging wound over the plantar aspect of her left foot for six months, along with a limp and pre-existing bilateral hallux valgus. Physical examination revealed a 4x5 cm wound with an active purulent sinus over the first metatarsal, inflammation, and limited painful movement of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Imaging (X-ray and MRI) showed an expansile osteolytic lesion with cortical thinning, a lytic lesion (16x19 mm) in the first metatarsal head and distal shaft, a bony sequestrum, and a sinus tract. Laboratory tests revealed a raised ESR (55 mm/hr), while other serological indicators were normal. Sputum AFB and CBNAAT were negative, and a chest radiograph was unremarkable, ruling out pulmonary involvement. Histopathological examination of the tissue from the lesion confirmed tuberculosis, showing epitheloid granulomas with caseating necrosis and lymphocytes. Following diagnosis, the patient was initiated on anti-tubercular treatment (four drugs initially, then three drugs for 10 months) and responded well within the first two months. Non-operative management was advised for the hallux valgus.
